Kenton Varda@KentonVarda · 11/26 03:26Cloudflare
Cloudflare Workers 技術負責人（Cap'n Proto 作者）
Worrying decision by Google to draw a distinction between agentic and deterministic API use, and require them to go through completely different APIs. Anything agent-driven will be required to use MCP, which is usually a poor fit for calling from code. Only deterministic code can use REST. In the future, this distinction will become increasingly impossible to make. Agents may write code and run it -- that's still agent-driven, seemingly. Agents may write code for humans to run -- that seems to be allowed to use REST. But more likely agents will be writing code that both agents and humans access together, in collaboration. I guess all such code will be required to use MCP. So I think the real effect of this decision is: Google REST APIs are deprecated. Only legacy apps can keep using them. In the future, nothing will be able to use them, because everything will be some amount agentic. Such uses must use MCP instead. Which would be fine if Google's MCP APIs provided everything their REST APIs do, but in general they do not. They are much narrower, designed to be consumed directly by agents, and designed to allow only the things that Google thinks third-party agents should be allowed to do. They offer no backwards-compatibility, so code written against them could break at any moment. I think this will backfire. If Google creates friction for people using agents, people will just stop using Google. All the Google Workspace apps can easily be slopforked at this point. https://t.co/BA7SNUJ1mQ
繁中摘要Kenton Varda 擔憂 Google 區分 agent 與確定性程式的 API 使用、要求 agent 一律走 MCP；他認為 agent 寫程式、人機協作越來越普遍，這種區分會越來越難成立。

notable that a lot of the recent anthropic (and ant-alum) talks have been very specific about how much there is still left to do for human engineers, and if you are feeling depressed/anxious you need only look here / point your efforts towards AGI-aligned problems*: - assume multiagent systems 1000x, from spawning subagents to being llm grader to advisor/sidekick pattern to dreaming/memory formation to collaborating peer to peer on a board. what breaks? - Infra: unbundle Kubernetes to new filesystems, sandboxing, stateful, fast workflow orchestration (see @temporalio) at crazy scale. it's actors on steroids. - Agent Authorization: EVERYONE agrees that having Instinct/Claude etc saving your password is bad (aka taking action On-Behalf-Of you instead of you delegating to an agent's own identity). Either you believe the AI buildout is over, that AI was a flash in the pan, and that the need for compute has already peaked... or this a rare buying opportunity. HBM and DRAM production is effectively sold out through 2029, with chip and memory supply projected to stay tight until well into the 2030s. AI research isn't slowing down: frontier training compute is doubling every ~5 months, and model capabilities are scaling over twice as fast as they did pre-reasoning. Anthropic Claude Code（前 Google Chrome 工程主管）
Code Mode is an experimental new feature in Claude Code that can improve both speed and context efficiency when Claude needs to orchestrate multiple steps. Try it out and let us know what you think! It enables Claude to perform multi-step tool calls by writing and running JavaScript. Rather than calling one tool at a time (e.g. Bash, Read, or Edit) and waiting to see the result before deciding what to do next, Code Mode allows Claude to write a simple script to run multiple commands in parallel, passing arguments and filtering outputs for subsequent tool calls to reduce context. I'm excited about this work because Code Mode enables more efficient and streamlined multi-step coding flows. For example, rather than passing large amounts of raw search data into the context window or having to make a large number of sequential calls to perform the same refactoring across dozens of files, Claude can orchestrate these tasks programmatically in a single pass. Still, you will be able to interact with Claude as normal through natural prompts. And if you ever need to see the exact JavaScript that Claude generated, you can always use Ctrl+O to expand the collapsed Code rows in the transcript viewer. One of the most exciting practical improvements from Code Mode is its ability to perform long-running operations, like running test suites or complex builds, as background processes. When Code Mode is running in either auto or bypassPermissions mode, scripts can run in the background for up to two hours. You can continue to interact with Claude and perform other work within the same session. The /tasks command provides complete transparency and control over background scripts. Each tool call that is generated within a script is still governed by your current deny and ask permission policies, sandbox constraints, and PreToolUse hooks. Hooks can even be defined specifically for the REPL tool to inspect the generated JavaScript before running, or redact sensitive tokens from the output before reading it into the context. To enable Code Mode, just start your session with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude or set the environment variable in your ~/.claude/settings.json file. Give it a try by running multi-file audits, batch edits, or any type of parallel search-and-filter operation. Code Mode is experimental and the team is actively iterating on it, so please run /feedback in your terminal to let us know what works well and where you hit any edges. Hope it's helpful!
繁中摘要Addy Osmani 介紹 Claude Code 實驗功能 Code Mode：讓 Claude 寫並執行 JavaScript 來串接多步工具呼叫，提升速度與 context 效率。

How my software factories use Vercel Board: 1. Vulnerability fixing factory: - We're syncing Linear tickets into the board as tasks - Nudging devs for approvals is a big part of getting things merged, so those are tracked on the board to prevent over-nudging - Inbound messages (comments on GH, Linear, replies to nudges) from devs are put on the board and processed by a dedicated agent to determine future actions - A needs-you board is used for agents to ask questions to the factory owners - Agents running on Vercel Sandboxes use a comms channel to communicate and give each other tasks. E.g. there is a dedicated agent that makes sure PRs stay green over time. - The board data is mined for a gamification dashboard (Thanks to @vvoyer for being number 1) 2. New secret project factory - This is a project focused on agent swarm hill-climbing - All agents log their decisions to a central board for knowledge sharing - When agents develop a hypothesis for an improvement as part of their work, they post it to the board for other agents to pick up - Each sandboxes log files are posted to the board and full agent traces are attached so that post-mortem debugging is fruitful - The factory has a daily run where it inspects the logs and traces to improve its own behavior - I'm currently interacting with the factory from claude, but all the sandboxes run fx. This type of inter-harness comms is just completely seamless with the board. - And much more. Screenshot attached over how the board is visualized. Notably, this is all prompted together and works just great. The agents just love using the board and the emergent behavior is delightful https://t.co/midwv0HqKS

Thorsten Ball@thorstenball · 11/20 00:30Amp
Amp coding agent；《Writing an Interpreter in Go》作者
Spaces might be the most controversial Amp feature we've ever launched. A lot of you immediately said: this is great, exactly what I wanted, love you, it's orbin' time my brother, etc. But others asked: "How do I use spaces? Is this not for me? Is it only for multiplayer?" What I find interesting about all of this is the meta observation that the conversation with a single agent is, in some way, "solved." Not a single question about that. Instead everybody is asking about how you hold the transcript: when do you start a new thread, do you use subthreads, when do you dive into subthreads vs. staying at high level, how do people collaborate with it, how do you organize them? And spaces hit right into this spaghetti web of opinions, approaches, and thoughts. And part of the confusion is ours. We thought of spaces like Slack channels: we have a Design space, a bug tracker space, and I have one for Boxes, where I shipped Boxes and now maintain and monitor them. And just like in Slack, the work still happens in threads, not in the main chat. But a lot of people interpreted spaces as chiefs of staff (and, frankly, our announcement didn't help): you talk to the main agent and never dive into the subthreads. That leads to disappointment when the main agent doesn't reply and they have to go into the subthread anyway. UI suggested this, agent does that. That, of course, begs the question: "well, Thorsten, if you don't have answers to all of these questions, why'd you ship spaces?" Three years ago I would have said we shouldn't have shipped it and polished and iterated more. But in 2026 everything can change in three weeks with a new model drop. It's, I think, important to hit the wave while you can and collect feedback. (Of course that was always true but with AI even more.) But it's also frothy and caused confusion (and delight!) and, in hindsight, I wish we'd underline the exploratory nature a bit more. We all believe the workflow of the future is a high abstraction layer, not micromanaging threads. But there's no denying you still have to go in, review things, and make sure what you told the agent to do is correct. Now our #1 goal internally is to match the UI and the agent's behavior to that.
繁中摘要Thorsten Ball 談 Amp 新功能 Spaces 的兩極反應，觀察到「和單一 agent 對話」似乎已被解決，大家問的都是怎麼管理對話紀錄：何時開新 thread、何時用子 thread。

Thorsten Ball@thorstenball · 11/19 02:44Amp
Amp coding agent；《Writing an Interpreter in Go》作者
Thoughts after talking to lots of engineers in London in last couple of days: • Everyone's moving into the same direction and getting more and more agent-pilled, but all on individual speed. No group of engineers right now is uniformly agent-pilled. • Becoming agent-pilled is a one-way door. You only realize this once you've gone through. Many think they "get it" but haven't made the switch yet. • Wild how many orgs are still treating agents as "thing that writes code on my computer" instead of robot-engineer that can help with whole SLDC. • Teams are drowning in PRs and code review. No process has been changed yet, even though this is the biggest dev productivity lever of last 30 years, engs still work off tickets like nothing happened. Wild. • Barely anyone realized yet that, hey, even if the model isn't good enough to write the code the way you'd write it [doubt it], they can surely write all of the peripheral tooling to speed you up. • Very few engineers have imagination to come up with better tool. Instead of reviewing code in diffs, line by line, think: if I could wave a magic wand and make tooling disappear, what tooling would I want to gain confidence in this change being correct? Full instrumented/traced end-to-end runthrough? Demo videos? In-production probes? High-fidelity and anonymized production data fed through test runs? New testing environments with the greatest debugging MCP support one can imagine so agent can inspect everything? It's time to dream big. But seems like most people's dreams don't reach further than "this agent works off the tickets assigned to me 10x faster than I can."
繁中摘要Thorsten Ball 在倫敦和大量工程師交流後的觀察：大家都在往 agent 化走但速度不一；許多組織仍把 agent 當寫程式工具、團隊被 PR 與 code review 淹沒，應該重新想像驗證變更的工具。

I’m being pitched a new inference neocloud company on average every two days. No exaggeration. I take every entrepreneur seriously and I look deeply into each. But it’s hard to fathom this being sustainable. At the same time, AI Gateway token demand on Vercel has been ~40% MoM compounded since the beginning of the year. No signs of stopping. One way to reconcile this is that compute is the new economy, and tokens the new energy unit. There’s a new Industrial Revolution taking place. Every aspect of our lives is being replatformed on top of this new system that enhances everything. More like an “oil rush” than a “gold rush”: it’s durable, not a fad. In the short term, I anticipate more expansion, followed by consolidation due to economies of scale, cybersecurity and enterprise requirements (ZDR and cyber being a hot topic for inference providers), capital requirements, and an evolving regulatory landscape.

Rex has really powerful Lua scripting that our beta group has been using to huge effect. We expanded it today with `rex.ui`: a way to build automations that require user interaction. The way this works with multiple clients: the choice pops up on all attached clients. The first client to respond wins (and hides the prompt from the rest). If any client is already showing a prompt, we respond with a "busy" error code and let the Lua script decide what it wants to do (sleep, try again, force it, etc.). This will surely improve, but the API gives us flexibility to improve it later. If no clients exist, another error code Lua can detect is returned noting that no user is attached, and it can decide what it wants to do.
繁中摘要Mitchell Hashimoto 介紹 Rex 的 Lua 腳本新增 rex.ui，可做需要使用者互動的自動化；多個 client 同時連線時，最先回應者勝出，忙碌或無人連線時回傳錯誤碼讓腳本自行處理。

Could be the start of a trend in new pre-training recipes: no LR decay phase anymore. (Also seen in Kolibri.) Instead: constant LR + averaging the last N checkpoints (or a running weight average). I guess that makes it easier in practice because you don't have to commit to a total training length upfront. A little meta analysis based on those who share training details: - Classic cosine: Llama 3, OLMo 2, OLMo 3, GLM-4.5, GLM-5, Kimi K3, Phi-4 - WSD ("Warmup-Stable-Decay"): DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek V4, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, Kimi K2, Kimi Linear, Nemotron 3 Nano, Nemotron 3 Super, SmolLM3, MiniMax M2 - No decay (constant LR plus checkpoint averaging): Kolibri-1, DatologyAI's models
繁中摘要Sebastian Raschka 觀察預訓練新趨勢：不再做學習率衰減，改用固定學習率加最後 N 個 checkpoint 平均，並整理各家模型用 cosine、WSD 或不衰減的做法。

devin bots are multi-agent teams done right: - always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI) - own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others) - manages teams of subagents (and reviews itself) - available everywhere (call text slack whatever hello @interaction) - consistent reporting thru interactive artifacts aka devinapps not long chats (HTML is all you need™ @trq212) this is the preview that @walden_yan gave at AIE. i've been trialing them for a week and i've been able to hand over my AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation, and video editing work (also simultaneously moving from local agent worktree hell to cloud because ofc this is all cloud based thank god) hyped concepts this replaces: - /goal - "ultracode" / "ultra mode" - "loop engineering" - "agent to agent" - "agent swarms" - AI employees (see below) my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol. if youre a startup, reminder that Devin for Startups offers 65k in credits. apply via clanker

Sebastian Raschka@rasbt · 11/16 22:28獨立
《Build a LLM From Scratch》作者
The open-source LLM ecosystem could really benefit from an LLM building-block API. We have so many LLM components across different models now. Whether you are using PyTorch or C++ and CUDA code directly, there is a major switching cost when you want to run experiments or ablation studies, say swapping GQA with MLA, dense FFNs with MoE, attention layers with Mamba2 or Gated DeltaNet, or standard residual connections with attention residuals. Currently, it’s very messy even with LLM-assisted coding. It could maybe be on top of PyTorch or CUDA directly, but it needs to be carefully engineered and maintained (versus quickly vibe-coded on a weekend) and efficient enough that people trust it to use in production (which is really a requirement to move beyond toy examples). Maybe some food for thought for a big, well-funded lab :) (There are some efforts that go into that direction, like torchtitan, torchtune, Megatron Core, OLMo-core, but they are not quite that level of abstraction, I'd say. And, as always, there’s the chicken-and-egg problem: it needs to be popular to get widely adopted, and it needs to get widely adopted to become popular.)
繁中摘要Sebastian Raschka 呼籲開源 LLM 生態需要一套「LLM 積木 API」，讓 GQA/MLA、MoE、Mamba2 等元件能低成本替換做實驗，而且要認真工程化維護。

Lucas Beyer@giffmana · 11/17 04:00Meta
Meta 研究員（前 OpenAI、DeepMind）
My way of contributing to PyTorch since I joined: complain and whine until something happens :D I was super happy by PyTorch team's reaction on this one! I complained about their current RNG API. I think it's horrible. I made a prototype of what I think it should look like, and we used that in our research codebase; but the implementation was horrible hacks on top of the current API. Then, I wrote a big doc explaining what I think the design should be like, and why, and how the current API simply doesn't allow it. I didn't hear much for a little while, but then they came back with a whole new design, largely the way I wanted it, plus some more. We iterated a little more on the rough edges of that (we iterated == I try it and complain), and here we are. (This is just my perspective, I'm sure there were others also requesting something like it, that I didn't see.) It's inspired by both NumPy's new API and JAX's API, but it also goes beyond both. I really like it; if you embrace the API, it gives you full control and awareness of PRNG in your codebase. It even forces you to think and make decisions you wouldn't have realized that you otherwise made implicitly, until they come back and bite you! This makes me think, maybe I should write a little guide/example of how to use it in some toy training codebase some time...
繁中摘要Lucas Beyer 分享推動 PyTorch 改 RNG API 的過程：做原型、寫長文說明設計，PyTorch 團隊最後推出大致照他想法的新設計。

Kenton Varda@KentonVarda · 11/13 00:25Cloudflare新
Cloudflare Workers 技術負責人（Cap'n Proto 作者）
In the late '90s I was a huge 3dfx fanboy. For a few years, they were so far ahead of everyone, making all other video cards look like jokes. I had a Voodoo 1, 2, and 3, and was excited for the Voodoo 5 with its promised full-screen anti-aliasing (FSAA). (I was in high school / starting college, a big gamer, and doing some OpenGL graphics programming as a hobby project.) The day the first GeForce was announced, though, I immediately recognized that 3dfx was toast. Like, immediately. Why? 3dfx had been entirely focused on maximizing fill rate. That is, given a set of textured triangles that are *already* specified in 2D screen space, the hardware would rasterize them as pixels. It was up to software to get the triangles into screen space in the first place, which mostly involves applying some matrix math to every vertex. But 3dfx figured there are way more pixel than vertices, and focusing on more pixels was the way to go to improve quality. With enough pixels they figured they could literally render every frame at 4x resolution and then down-sample to make the edges smoother (FSAA). The Voodoo 5 was a monstrous brute force design whose top-end version had four copies of the chip in order to render those four pixels at the same time. The GeForce, on the other hand, went ahead and moved vertices into hardware. The result? It could render an order of magnitude more triangles, which meant surfaces could be smoother. It was immediately obvious that this had a far bigger impact than FSAA, both from the screenshots and from what I'd been learning about graphics programming. A friend of mine (who still attends my LAN parties today) was staying with us at the time. I remember going over to his computer while he was out, loading up the screenshots from the announcement, and leaving a little note in a text editor about how I'd switched allegiance. Of course, games did not get the benefit automatically. Engines had to be rewritten to move their vertex handling into hardware, whereas 3dfx's brute force and FSAA would immediately apply to existing games. This is why 3dfx's bet was the easy one to make, and Nvidia's so much harder. But Nvidia has continued making these bets, over and over, ever since. They have repeatedly built for markets that didn't exist yet, investing in stuff that would take many years to pay off. CUDA when nobody was asking for it. Ray tracing when nobody was asking for it. Almost every generation of Nvidia hardware has something qualitatively new. Jensen calls these "zero-billion-dollar markets". Doing this requires leadership. The natural state of a big company is to focus on whatever incremental improvements their biggest customers are asking for, because those are the easiest decisions to justify. It works great for a while, then fails. That's the Innovator's Dilemma. And even executives who have read the book find it hard to internalize. Even executives hand-picked by the CEO who has internalized it often cannot themselves internalize it. It's weirdly hard to find leadership that gets it, and no amount of bottom-up innovation can make up for it. And that's why I sold my Nvidia stock this morning.
繁中摘要回憶 90 年代末當 3dfx 鐵粉：Voodoo 1/2/3 一度遙遙領先，曾期待 Voodoo 5 的全螢幕反鋸齒。

What happens to frameworks in the agents era? to component libraries? to @shadcn? The answer is: we need to drill deeper. Delete the part, optimize, accelerate, automate. UI SDK is like the x86 instruction set for agents to build new UI components spontaneously. Agents are the new design engineers, and they're ready to build *anything* you ask, tailored to your usecase. High-level, rigid, single-framework abstractions are like kryptonite for what is essentially an infinite, untiring creation machine. I think we've found someone that allows us to have the cake and eat it too. A decades-long dream. UI SDK is packaged behaviors that give us accessibility, performance, cohesion, saving us tokens, errors and effort, but with absolutely zero limitations and tradeoffs for what UIs we can generate. Enjoy!

libghostty-vt 1.0.1 released. ABI stable so its a drop-in upgrade. Biggest highlight is that we provide prebuilt Windows builds now (DLL and static libs)! Windows builds here: https://t.co/qu9Folb0NB ("Windows") Highlights - Prebuilt Windows builds. Releases now include zips for x86_64 and aarch64 (Windows on Arm), each with the DLL, import and static libraries, headers, CMake and pkg-config files. - Faster memory operations on Linux. Builds that dynamically link glibc now use its memset, memcpy and memmove, which pick the best CPU features at runtime and beat Zig's compiler_rt in every benchmark we have. - Fixed garbled input with an AVX-512 system. Performance - Setting a scrollback line limit now performs the same as a byte limit. We're still so small but I'm loving the team we've got at Superlogical. They're so talented and kind and love their craft. It's a different era of software development and our expectations and practices reflect that. I want to share a bit about how we work. First, everyone is trusted to push to main. We do machine-aided code review pre-push and human plus more machine-aided code review post-push. Limited to no PRs. Culturally, we've all agreed that if we ever hire someone who we DON'T trust to push directly to main, then they probably aren't the right fit for the team (so far, not an issue). Some common sense here: if someone is stepping outside their lane or comfort zone, we'll open PRs. For example, I'm pretty trash at macOS/iOS UI, so I'll open PRs for UI-affecting functionality and ask for eyeballs/help. But for business logic and internals, I push to main. Second, everyone can cut a release. Our release process is fully automated and when you start a release (for any platform) it triggers a Slack notification and a 15 minute countdown. The 15 minute warning is a final gate that allows people to review plus collaborate on a changelog. During that 15 minutes, anyone in the company can pause the release rollout. After 15 minutes, the train leaves the station. You can't override the 15 minutes (except to pause). It gives everyone a chance to step in. Third, we avoid synchronization through fast remediation rather than through planning. The server and clients on various platforms ship features as fast as they can. We use post-hoc human review and AI-assistance to identify feature mismatches across products ("Windows has support for X and Mac doesn't." or "Mac and Windows differ in their behaviors for Y in this way."). This avoids expensive "sync" meetings and coordination. We trust that producers of features are mindful of what they're producing and we trust that adjacent product lines will self-synchronize quickly. In practice, we see feature parity across platforms within 24 to 48 hours. All of this works on mutual trust. It ONLY works with mutual trust. Everyone at all times has to trust that they've got each others back: 1. Push to main only works if you fix your mess, or if you don't, that someone else will quickly but that you'd do the same (and generally in equal amounts). 2. Anyone can deploy only works if you trust everyone to cut at the right time, with the right changelog, and that people will respect the 15 minute timer. 3. Sync through fast remediation only works if you trust other teams will pick up and integrate your work quickly, which only works if you would too. It also only works if you are fairly producing mismatches (e.g. not constantly). We've got a great team. I know we're still small and that these practices will change in many ways as we scale. But this is already a markedly different practice than what I would've done 15 years ago. In general, we are building from day 1 on a foundation of mutual respect, excellence, and trust. And it's been awesome.
繁中摘要分享 Superlogical 的工作方式：人人可直接 push 到 main（機器輔助 review，幾乎不開 PR）、人人可發版（15 分鐘倒數可暫停），用快速補救取代同步會議，一切建立在互信上。

Sebastian Raschka@rasbt · 11/11 00:30獨立
《Build a LLM From Scratch》作者
Currently working towards a bigger open LLM roundup. But in the meantime, just one of the interesting trends that stood out. I.e., looks like the transition from full to hybrid attention continues. In 2025, there were still lots of full attention models, with a shift to "some full attention" hybrids. In the first half of 2026, the trend towards "some full attention" hybrids continued. And now, in the second half of 2026, we have a 50/50 split between "some full attention" hybrids and models that don't use full attention at all anymore. And yes, there are also no full attention models anymore. The plot legend here means, - Full attention throughout = Global MHA, GQA, dense MLA, CCA in EVERY layer. - Some full attention = Full global attn mixed with: sliding-window/chunked attention, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, Mamba-2, Lightning Attention, convolutions, sparse attention. - No full attention = Zero dense global layers. The main implication is that the trend goes towards making long contexts cheaper to use. This means, it makes the architectures more suitable for long documents and conversations, large code bases, and of course agent usecases that rely on a lot of tool calls. In particular, there are two distinct efficiency gains here: 1) Less attention computation, since sparse attention and the like select tokens or blocks from the context and performs the expensive attention operation from only that subset. (Note that it can still retrieve information from distant positions.) 2) Less memory for retaining context in some architectures, meaning that recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet maintain a fixed-size state. Of course, this saves memory, but compressing the history creates challenges for exact retrieval, so they are usually intermixed with traditional attention methods (sparse or full).
繁中摘要整理開放 LLM 架構趨勢：全注意力模型已消失，2026 下半年「部分全注意力」混合架構與「完全無全注意力」各佔一半，目標是讓長上下文與 agent 用例更便宜。

So bullish on MCP. Its utility exceeds the "M" part: even AI aside, it'll be a civilization-scale accomplishment to get all our systems communicating through one universal open protocol. sunil pai@threepointone · 11/10 02:22獨立（PartyKit）
前 Cloudflare agents／PartyKit
If by "Software Factory" you mean another grandiose name for a collection of scripts, loops, and workflows, invented by people who need something new to put in their pitch decks, a phrase designed to get developers excited and VCs to open their wallets, a bandwagon for people who have discovered cron jobs and would now like to raise a Series A, then I am against Software Factories. But if by "Software Factory" you mean a real and rather interesting change in how software gets built, where engineers who were previously using agents to write features and fix bugs are now building systems that get agents to do those things autonomously, where the engineer has moved up a layer of abstraction, from working on the product to working on the machinery that builds the product, then I am for Software Factories. Because that's the distinction I'm interested in. We're no longer just using agents to build software. We're building the thing that uses agents to build software. You can call them loops. You can call them workflows. You can call them whatever you like. But "Software Factory" seems as good a name as any, and I rather like the idea that we're no longer merely product engineers, but factory engineers. This is my stand. I will not compromise.
繁中摘要吐槽「Software Factory」一詞：不過是一堆腳本、迴圈與工作流的浮誇新名字，用來讓開發者興奮、讓 VC 掏錢。

libghostty 1.0 is here! I started Ghostty ~5yrs ago to work towards this. Today, libghostty is in hundreds of projects used by tens of millions of people. 1.0 marks ABI stability, quality, and an invite for distros to begin packaging. https://t.co/i0FoSZHJT3 Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". Today, I'll answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had. On top of JetBrains and Neovim already mentioned (that alone being over 10 million users): -KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. - Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. - devenv uses it to drive shells. - Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. -Ghostel brings it to Emacs. - ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. - Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. - And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux, have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator. I'm excited to see where people take it from here.

I unironically agree with @bcherny’s take that “coding is solved, but bugs are not.” The deeper meaning is that you can in theory code *anything* now. You can burn infinite tokens refining and optimizing. Including optimizations that no one will care about 💀 With Vercel you can build a different kind of recursive improvement loop. You capture traces from production, you then optimize and course-correct based on how your software is being used IRL. This is not a new idea. The best engineers I’ve ever worked with never jumped into coding (now prompting) right away. You instrument the system, collect data, understand distributions, user journeys, and then put fingers on keyboard. You can ask your agent today to look at your traces!

while i'm quite bullish on formal methods, i think it's worth tempering expectations and doing your own research on it (disclaimer: i am not an expert in it). it cannot guarantee your code is bug free, only that it matches the spec under certain assumptions, and the specs come from what people want, not math. as long as we build software for humans, nothing can prove that your spec is right, only you can judge. i created the /statechart skill in pstack primarily because it helps make the state machines implicit in your code more obvious and legible to you, so you can shrink the review surface and review the work at a higher level: does it actually match your intent and goal? i used this skill a ton while building my game https://t.co/sa18sM28uD, below you can see the statechart for story mode where i was able to find many bugs with it. in that sense, i think model checking (eg TLA+ with TLC) is quite useful for understanding and checking properties of your system e2e, and you don't have to write tons of new verification code for it. the spec isn't your actual code so there's always a risk of drift, but so far i've had good experiences finding actual bugs with it. i tend to pair it with empirical verification (running the code) also to confirm it's real other types of formal verification like proving theorems (eg Lean, Dafny), bounded model checking (eg CBMC, Kani) etc have their own tradeoffs. proofs cover every possible input, but only for the properties specified, and it takes a lot more code/work. bounded model checking can run on your actual code, which avoids drift, but it only checks up to a certain number of steps, so it's better at finding bugs than proving there aren't any so i think in the near-medium term you'll still need to layer your codebase: constraints and guardrails (types, lint rules, api design, refactoring), empirical verification (tests, evals, real usage), and formal verification for the parts that really need it. none of these catch everything on their own, but layered together, they catch a lot more and shrink what's left for you to review but also maybe in the limit, the bitter lesson will prevail and flawless code will just be printed out perfectly every time with no bugs. even in that scenario, /statechart still seems very helpful in confirming that the agent understood your intent correctly. give it a try if you haven't already! https://t.co/9erGZLOzxO

The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds for Physical AI. Most embodied prediction tasks like object localization, robot trajectory planning, and dense 3D motion are fixed-length float vectors. For example, a bounding box is always 6 tokens, a 10-waypoint robot arm trajectory is 54: we know these beforehand. Instead of decoding one token at a time, we can output the entire geometric shape in one go. VFlash enables up to 12x faster action decoding and a 5.1x overall robot inference speedup on edge GPUs like the Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. What’s surprising is that it ends up even more accurate than the VLM backbone, with up to 61% lower 3D trajectory error. The intuition is that VFlash avoids the cascading errors of autoregressive decoding, where every coordinate is written in ink and every later point loses the chance to backspace. Everything that moves will be autonomous, and everything autonomous will need to think on its own chip. The next inference revolution is physical reasoning at the speed of reflex. And as always, it’s open paper, open source! Link in thread:

An update on building games with Claude Code: Last week some of you ran into Claude Code pushing back on game projects it should have just built. We'd added a short rule to the Opus 5.5 prompt to steer Claude away from recreating specific existing games, but it was also kicking in when you referenced one just to describe the mechanics you wanted. We've updated that rule in 2.1.317. You can name a game to describe what you want and Claude should now build an original game in that genre. If you ask for a copy of the original, it'll offer to build something similar instead. We want Claude to be as helpful as possible when you're building something original, but also to protect your work if someone else tries to copy it. We'll keep improving this, so let us know if Claude turns down work that's yours. Thanks to everyone who shared feedback!

Sebastian Raschka@rasbt · 11/03 23:19獨立
《Build a LLM From Scratch》作者
Catching up on the 10 (!) open LLM architecture releases from the past month. Quite a lot happened in October. I guess we can call it "Open October"! 1. Kolibri-1 (78B): A notable model from Germany. Features classic Grouped Query Attention (GQA) and Sliding Window Attention (SWA) attention module. 2. Ling 3.1 Flash (560B): Uses Kimi Delta Attention and the eighth uses gated Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) inspired by DeepSeek. 3. Muse Spark Open (816B): Besides Musse Glimmer, the first major open weight release from Meta (since Llama). Uses classic GQA + SWA but adds a LatentMoE. 4. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (120B): Combines Mamba-2 layers with just eight attention layers. Also LatentMoE 5. Dory1.0 (4B): A looped transformer design. 6. Reflection Beam (501B): GQA+SWA architecture. 7. Recursive Flint (40B): Note that "Recursive" is the company name; the architecture is a fairly standard MoE with GQA and SWA. 8. MiniMax M3.1-Flash (428B): Uses their own MiniMax Sparse Attention module. 9. LFM3 (1.7B): Hybrid architecture that mixes short convolutions and attention. 10. Mistral Large 4 (1T) combines MLA with sparse attention. Will probably cover/discuss things in more depth in the coming weeks!

A quick note. On both Linux and macOS, libghostty already processes data faster than the kernel can supply it over a pty fd. Ghostty is literally the floor of how fast `cat` can get (over plain text). So the plain ASCII/Unicode improvements here do NOT translate to visible `cat` speed differences. The speedups aren't for nothing though: they are visible in real-world mixed-data throughput because some sequences still can't be processed faster than a kernel read, so if libghostty is e.g. stalled handling some slow OSC, we'll catch back up much faster when we hit plain text runs. Also, for non-pty reads such as direct files or direct from memory, e.g. on stored or generated output, libghostty can process this data according to the speed increases shown below. I've enjoyed the `cat` benchmark for a long time, but I am sad to say its done. We've finished it. It can't get any faster without kernel changes.
繁中摘要說明 libghostty 在 Linux 與 macOS 上處理資料已比核心透過 pty 供應還快，所以純文字的效能改進不會反映在 cat 速度上。

Mitchell Hashimoto@mitchellh · 11/04 01:13Ghostty（前 HashiCorp）
Ghostty 作者；Terraform、Vagrant 作者
libghostty has always been fast, but it's also been getting significantly faster. Here are IO throughput measurements comparing Ghostty 1.3.1, 1.4.0, and main as of this morning. We'll be backporting most of these to a 1.4.1 release soon. Here are some highlights of the changes since 1.4: - Ghostty 1.4 had a fast-path for printing runs of plain text. But the fast-path only applied to limited cases. We now support mixed width characters and hyperlinks in the fast path. - Our input path always widened the pty data to codepoints (8-bit to 32-bit) as part of UTF-8 decode, which also incurred a memory copy. We now have a SIMD fast path to detect pure-ASCII and we process the run direct from the read buffer (no copy, narrower data). - New memory pages use most recent two pages actual utilization to pre-size themselves accordingly. This sped up styles, hyperlinks etc. - When a VM page runs out of capacity for a certain type of data (e.g. hyperlinks, styles), we now project the usage so far to guess what you'll need, then shrink available rows to avoid a realloc. Before we'd naively double. This caused a classic "laddering" problem. - We recognized "erase" being a slow path for us, and it's a common sequence, so we use another bit in row headers to track blank (we had space). - Styles are now processed once per SGR. Previously, a sequence like "ESC[1;38;2;r;g;bm" would apply each style as it came in (1, then 38, then 2, etc.). We now apply all attributes at once and write to the cursor atomically. - Styles are now packed into 128-bit values and use aarch64 and x86_64-specific assembly for minimizing instructions to use it. - On x86_64, we found that LLVM was lowering some row resets (hot path) to a 4-byte store followed by an 8-byte load which couldn't be store-forwarded. This caused an almost 10% (!!!) slowdown on scroll operations only on x86_64. The fix was to change our reset to build the full header in a register then do a single memmove per row. Net results are what you see in the graph, but written out main to 1.4: ASCII 1.5x, heavy styling 1.5x, styled Unicode 1.8x, random UTF-8 1.4x, random OSC 8 2.7x, mixed styled text with links 4.8x, cursor/erase 16x, hyperlink-dense text 5.6x.
繁中摘要公布 Ghostty 1.3.1、1.4.0 與 main 的 IO 吞吐量比較，大部分改進會回移到即將推出的 1.4.1。

John Carmack@ID_AA_Carmack · 10/30 23:06Keen Technologies（前 Oculus）
AGI 研究；id Software 創辦人
I am hesitant to weigh in on discussions about 30+ year old details. I understand enough about memory in general, and mine in particular, to not have great confidence about it. I generally trust Romero’s memory more than mine — I was always a bit jealous of that capability. In broad terms, multiplayer gaming was right up there with 3D gaming in my grand visions of what I wanted to accomplish. The early FPS games were very much “first person Gauntlet”, and Gauntlet had multiplayer. I do clearly remember the first time I got two computers running Doom taking to each other. Moving around on one computer and seeing the character move on the other screen was sublime. And then, of course, I shot the other character. Every shared virtual environment inhabited by young men inevitably hosts deathmatch. I suspect the confusion here may be around the fraction of people that originally bought Doom because of multiplayer. It was almost certainly well under 10%. Maybe under 1%. It wrecked some college networks, but most people didn’t have Ethernet cards or null modem cables. We probably did have some conversations correctly predicting that. Deathmatch was awesome, but most of our players never got to experience it. Even four games later for Quake 3 Arena, being “deathmatch focused” was a huge internal battle, and not at all obviously viable.
繁中摘要Carmack 回憶 Doom 初期：多人連線和 3D 一樣是他的大願景，但當年買 Doom 為了多人模式的人大概不到 10%，甚至不到 1%；到 Quake 3 Arena 主打 deathmatch 仍是內部大爭論。

AGI 研究；id Software 創辦人
AI may well be able to write massive software projects “from scratch”, but that almost certainly isn’t the fastest / highest performance / highest security / most token efficient way to do things. Good building blocks matter. In addition to RL’ing the agents on final task loss, we should try to get them to regularize the building blocks as well. What would the standard library look like that makes the agents most effective? It is likely at the limit that it turns out to be some alien organization of code, but given the existing human-bias in training, I bet that in the near term it would be lovely code that old programmers would appreciate. I suspect the same could be said for mathematics, but that is out of my lane.
繁中摘要Carmack 認為 AI 從零寫大型專案不是最快、最安全或最省 token 的做法，好的基礎元件很重要；應該也訓練 agent 規範化底層元件，想像最適合 agent 的標準函式庫長什麼樣。

Thorsten Ball@thorstenball · 10/30 01:05Amp
Amp coding agent；《Writing an Interpreter in Go》作者
Next question: why are you still using branches? We talked about PRs. I don't think they make sense anymore, if you rethink them from first principles. Yes, if you only use them to trigger CI, then sure, go ahead. That's a fat commit, not a PR. But for mandatory code review? Knowledge sharing? C'mon. But some of you said: "we use PRs because we use branches! I love to keep my stuff on branches." And I'm here to tell you: you don't need branches! You can just push to main. It's called trunk-based development and the idea behind it is true continuous integration: you continuously integrate your changes with the trunk, the main branch. It's been around for a while, it works. Just yesterday I talked with someone who said they've used it in an org with 400 engineers, without any issues. Ruby, the project, uses trunk-based development. The main idea is that you want to avoid long-lived branches. They're bad, because branches can diverge and merging can turn into a thing. And you don't want routine operations to become a thing. Even when I worked in teams that used PRs and branches, I considered it a smell when a branch lived for longer than a day or two. But when I shared this with others, I'd often get something back like this: "Well, good for you, but no. MY thing, what I'm working on, that can't be done on main. It needs to be on a branch! It has a database migration, it changes the underlying shape, the architecture, it refactors this and changes that. It can't go on main yet! I need to merge it all at the end." And then I'd say: "Nah, I can merge nearly anything continuously in small commits to main. You split things up. Add the column first, merge that, deploy it, now it's out, works, safe. Add the helpers first, merge them, get them out. Want to migrate from legacy pattern A to new pattern B? Don't do it all at once. Add the dependency, then migrate A to B, one by one, safe." If it can be merged in a large change, I bet it can be done in small increments that you merge to main. Yes, there are exceptions, but it's 0.5% of cases, not 50%. But there was a real problem with this approach: it was hard! There's a lot of "meta programming" you have to do: make sure this small first change compiles and runs and the tests work, merge it, get it out, monitor it; then do the next small piece, make sure that works and get it out; then maybe push some still-unused dead code, add a feature flag, add a config variable; or keep both configurations working at the same time, etc. That meant sometimes it was just easier to do it in a big fat branch. But big fat branches are risky! A system that continuously flows is safer than a system that starts and stops in spurts. But -- you guessed it -- here's the good news: Now, with agents, all of these chores are no chores at all! Agents are great at adding feature flags, they're great at splitting up code, they're great at keeping track of three changes and merging them one by one and watching them roll out. They're great at keeping two configurations working for a day. They're great at migrating one by one. In other words: it's now 10x easier to just work on main and make sure everything is continuously integrated and working. It's now easy to make sure the system constantly flows. And look, ... I'm not here to convince you to switch to trunk-based development. Just a ruse to get you to read this. (But also, hey: try it! Pushing to main is amazing.) I'm here to make you RETHINK how you develop software. Don't just use agents to replace your typing. Use agents as the magic code-writing machines they are. Everything that was hard about software development because it involved writing code -- even the meta programming -- has become easier. You can now reach for the stars! But you need to look up.
繁中摘要Thorsten Ball 長文主張不用分支、直接推 main（trunk-based development）：以前拆小步提交很麻煩，現在 agent 很會加 feature flag、拆改動、逐步遷移，持續整合變得容易十倍。
